title: ‘The Unknown’ Director Arthur Harari Says AI Is a ‘Slippery Slope,’ Though He ‘Had to Use Deepfake Tool’ for Léa Seydoux Double Scene: ‘There Was a Human Behind It’
description: “The Unknown” filmmaker Arthur Harari says AI is a “slippery slope” and one he’d prefer to avoid in his own work — even as he admitted on Sunday at
body:
“The Unknown” filmmaker Arthur Harari says AI is a “slippery slope” and one he’d prefer to avoid in his own work — even as he admitted on Sunday at the Marrakech Film Festival that he used a deepfake tool in his Palme d’Or contender, a body-swap psychodrama starring Léa Seydoux.

	Appearing in conversation with film critic and historian Charles Tesson, the Oscar-winning “Anatomy of a Fall” co-writer was asked by an audience member how he viewed the role of AI technology in his creative process.
	

	“I’m in much the same position as everyone else: this shift toward using AI is suddenly upon us, and it’s becoming not just a possibility, but something increasingly pervasive and tempting,” Harari said. “Personally, I’ve never used it; for the time being, I don’t see any place for it in my work.”

	The acclaimed writer-director went on to walk that statement back moments later, when he admitted that his team employed deepfake technology for a pivotal scene in his latest film.

	“At one point in ‘The Unknown,’ there is a scene where Léa Seydoux kisses Léa Seydoux, and we had to use a deepfake tool to do that,” he said. “But there was a human behind it. There was always a human involved — someone who programs it, so to speak, and keeps it under control. So, I’m not against it in principle. It’s just that I think we need to ask ourselves what constitutes the essence of what we’re trying to create — right from the writing stage.”

	As a writer, Harari appeared to be more resistant to the technology, conceding that AI tools were “perfectly legitimate and interesting” when it comes to performing simple research tasks. But to go beyond that — “to actually craft parts of the writing process” — was, he insisted, “a very slippery slope.”
	

	“The thing is, we are inherently prone to addiction — look at our phones, for instance; we’re constantly glued to them,” he said. “Once you get a foot in the door, it becomes incredibly difficult not to use it at every turn.”

	Premiering in competition at this year’s Cannes Film Festival, “The Unknown” stars Seydoux as an unknown woman who has a one-night stand with a photographer named David (Niels Schneider). When David wakes up, he’s trapped inside Seydoux’s body. The film was based on a graphic novel co-written by Harari.

	Speaking to Variety earlier this year, the French actress described the role as “the best part I’ve ever played.” Asked if she thought AI would put filmmakers out of business, she replied, “I don’t think so. I think that nothing can replace humanity. I don’t feel threatened. Maybe I’m wrong! But I believe in human nature.”

	Harari is on hand at the Marrakech Film Festival as part of its popular Conversation series. He’s appearing alongside “Knives Out” director Rian Johnson, “Call Me by Your Name” Oscar nominee Luca Guadagnino, “Fjord” Palme d’Or winner Cristian Mungiu, Italian screen icon Monica Bellucci and more.

	The Marrakech Film Festival runs Nov. 20–28.

schema.headline: ‘The Unknown’ Director Arthur Harari Says AI Is a ‘Slippery Slope,’ Though He ‘Had to Use Deepfake Tool’ for Léa Seydoux Double Scene: ‘There Was a Human Behind It’

title: J.A. Bayona, Guneet Monga Kapoor, Vikas Khanna Board Student Academy Award Winner ‘The Dragon Letter’ as Director Plans Feature Version (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Spanish director J.A. Bayona, Oscar-winning producer Guneet Monga Kapoor and Michelin-starred chef and filmmaker Vikas Khanna have come aboard shor
body:
Spanish director J.A. Bayona, Oscar-winning producer Guneet Monga Kapoor and Michelin-starred chef and filmmaker Vikas Khanna have come aboard short “The Dragon Letter” as executive producers, and Ladakhi director Stanzin Jigmet tells Variety he is developing a feature version of the Student Academy Award-winning short.

	The film was named the narrative Gold winner at the 53rd Student Academy Awards, and has been entered in the live action short race for the 99th Academy Awards. Spain’s ESCAC Films produced it in association with India Sikhya Entertainment, with shooting split between Ladakh and Barcelona.
	

	Bayona was born in Barcelona, the city where Jigmet trained, and made his first feature with “The Orphanage.” He went on to direct “The Impossible,” “A Monster Calls,” “Jurassic World: Fallen Kingdom” and “Society of the Snow.”

	“What I find so beautiful about ‘The Dragon Letter’ is how a deeply personal story, rooted in a remote corner of the Himalayas, can speak to something universal: friendship, kindness, and the courage to find your own voice,” Bayona said.

	“That, to me, is the magic of cinema. It brings us together, helps us make sense of our own little worlds, and gives us a language through which we can understand one another. The more deeply we explore what makes us unique, the more we discover what connects us to the rest of the world. Sometimes, the most universal stories are born in the most unexpected places.”

	A BAFTA nominee who co-founded Sikhya Entertainment, the Mumbai banner, Monga Kapoor won the documentary short Oscar in 2023 alongside director Kartiki Gonsalves for “The Elephant Whisperers,” the first Indian production to take that award. She was also an executive producer on “Period. End of Sentence.,” which won in the same category in 2019. France has made her a Chevalier de l’Ordre des Arts et des Lettres, and she set up Women in Film India to support women and gender-diverse professionals in the country’s screen sector.
	

	“What moved me most about ‘The Dragon Letter’ is its beautiful message about childhood friendship. When you’re young, a friend who helps you with your homework or draws a dragon for you can make you feel understood in a way that stays with you for life. Stanzin captures that tenderness so honestly and reminds us how those small acts of kindness can give children the confidence to find their own voice. I’m delighted to come on board as executive producer and help share his film with audiences around the world,” Monga Kapoor said.

	For an independent filmmaker, Jigmet tells Variety, Monga Kapoor brings ties to publicists and a working knowledge of awards campaigns. “She has lots of experience and such a personality in championing this independent cinema and taking it to international stages. I’m really grateful that Guneet joined my project as an executive producer and helping us a lot,” he says.

	Khanna, who was raised in Amritsar, runs the kitchen at Bungalow in New York and is a judge on “MasterChef India.” He has published 36 books and made several documentaries, and his Feed India initiative has helped provide millions of meals. His first feature as director, “The Last Color,” starred Neena Gupta and centered on a friendship that grows between an older widow and a young tightrope walker in Varanasi.

	“I love the way he shows how children look after one another in ways adults might barely notice,” Khanna said.

	The story centers on Skarma (Jigmet Spalchen), a 10-year-old who is asked to pen a note to his Barcelona sponsor. Every child in the class is supposed to copy out the same text and sketch the same dragon. Skarma has other ideas about what to say. The question is whether he can summon the nerve to write them down.

	The film draws on Jigmet’s own years at a Himalayan boarding school. Many of his friends there had sponsors in Europe and had to send them a thank-you letter every year. Jigmet would decorate those letters with a dragon, including for classmates who helped with his schoolwork.

	He wrote the script at ESCAC in Barcelona, where every student on his master’s program had to pitch a story to the school. Being in Spain already suited the project, since its final section had to be filmed in Europe.

	Jigmet comes from Mulbekh, a Himalayan village without a cinema. “I grew up very far from the industry, so in Ladakh I learned filmmaking from YouTube only,” he says. In 2021 he launched Ladakh-based Pixel Challenger Films, making ads and public awareness films, and he also worked on Vidhu Vinod Chopra’s “12th Fail.” A few of his narrative commercials went viral, and ESCAC got in touch offering him a scholarship for a master’s in film directing.
	

	One of his professors there told the class: “Never do films with kids and dogs. You are going to struggle a lot.” Jigmet went on to write a film with 75 children in it.

	The Barcelona shoot, with a professional crew and professional actors, was “like a luxury for me,” he says. Ladakh was another matter. There he worked with non-actors, an entire school of children and a very small team. Equipment was scarce, and local kids pitched in by holding the lights. Having grown up in the Himalayas within that culture, Jigmet says, he was able to draw natural performances from his young cast.

	Jigmet lensed the Ladakh scenes himself and also edited the film. Miguel Esteban Alonso handled cinematography for the Barcelona unit. Sergi Casamitjana and Aintza Serra produced for ESCAC Films, with Pixel Challenger Films participating. Jigmet Wangial, Rosa Nicolás, Ferran Devick and Urgain Phuntsog round out the cast. Victor H. L. Bruneau was line producer, Natali Gutierrez production designer and Sebastián Orueta Murillo sound designer.

	Sikhya, a Jio Studios company, has backed titles including “The Lunchbox,” “Masaan,” “Pagglait” and “Kill,” along with Indian National Film Award winners “Kathal – A Jackfruit Mystery” and “Soorarai Pottru.” Its latest theatrical releases are Karthik Subbaraj’s “Dorothy” and “Udta Teer,” the first feature from writer-director Akash Kaushik.

	For now, Jigmet is busy with the short’s Oscar campaign. “But I’m also developing a feature version of ‘The Dragon Letter.’ That’s the plan,” he says.

	Jigmet is currently attending the WAVES Film Bazaar, the market component of the International Film Festival of India in Goa.

schema.headline: J.A. Bayona, Guneet Monga Kapoor, Vikas Khanna Board Student Academy Award Winner ‘The Dragon Letter’ as Director Plans Feature Version (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Mahershala Ali Says It ‘Doesn’t Matter’ That He’s Won 2 Oscars Because ‘There Are Not Roles for Me’ in ‘the Vast Majority of Projects’: ‘You’re Like Everybody Else Waiting’
description: Mahershala Ali got candid about the impact — or lack thereof — his two Oscar wins have had on his career in Hollywood while appearing on a recent e
body:
Mahershala Ali got candid about the impact — or lack thereof — his two Oscar wins have had on his career in Hollywood while appearing on a recent episode of Carmelo Anthony and Kazeem “Kaz” Famuyide’s “7PM in Brooklyn” podcast.

	The actor, who took home trophies for best supporting actor for both 2018’s “Greenbook” and 2016’s “Moonlight,” asked the hosts about the meaning of an Oscar, and if it really validates whether someone is “a good actor” or not. “There’s more good actors than there is good material,” he said. “It’s not even that all these people are competing for these same spots. It’s just that out of all the material made, there’s only a handful of them that check certain boxes.”
	

	He continued: “The vast majority of projects that get greenlit, there are not roles for me in those. You gotta think that way, you know what I mean? So, it doesn’t matter if I got 17 Oscars. If someone is not writing something for you or greenlighting something with you in mind, you’re like everybody else waiting and looking and searching.”

	While the star noted that actors could produce their own projects, the timeline is usually as least a “three to five year” journey. When asked by Famuyide if an Oscar win validates Black actors, Ali responded: “It’s kind of just talk. It doesn’t translate to anything real. You don’t want to find yourself in a situation where, oh, that’s ‘the diversity project.’ You just want to do great material as a Black person. You’re not thinking of yourself as this exotic other, per se. You just are living your life.”
	

	Most recently, Ali starred in Bassam Tariq’s “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother,” which hit theaters on Sept. 25. Tariq was also the original director of Marvel’s failed “Blade” movie, in which Ali was set to star in the title role, which he recently discussed in an interview with The New Arab.

	“It was funny and strange to start casting and building without a proper script,” Tariq told interviewer Hanna Flint about his short-lived Marvel career. “You’re sitting there and explaining to actors what their role will be, and they just have to believe you. That’s also very dangerous because if the text comes and it doesn’t add up to what you were saying, your credibility gets completely shot. All I have is my integrity, and I’ve been thinking about that a lot.”

	“If you’re the bearer of bad news to your actors, but you’re not the one making any of these decisions — and it’s actually coming from a corporate entity — that’s not a great way to be a director,” he continued. “I know some people can take that and run with it, but I learned I was losing credibility with my actors, and it wasn’t a healthy way to operate as a filmmaker. Life’s too short to make shit films, so that was my big lesson: I have to have full control over my script. If we disagree, it’s between them and me. It’s quite sad because we had such high hopes for what we wanted to build.”

	Speaking of the film’s inability to get made, Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige had previously said he felt “like a gigantic loser and failure,” a statement that Ali agreed with in a GQ interview in the months following. “To this day, I don’t know why it didn’t happen. I just know that it was—Kevin, he said it was the biggest failure of his career and I agree,” said Ali.

schema.headline: Mahershala Ali Says It ‘Doesn’t Matter’ That He’s Won 2 Oscars Because ‘There Are Not Roles for Me’ in ‘the Vast Majority of Projects’: ‘You’re Like Everybody Else Waiting’

title: Kieran Culkin Says a ‘Succession’ Spinoff ‘Would Be a Terrible Idea’: ‘What Are You Hoping For? “Cousin Greg: The Sitcom?”’
description:
Sorry, “Succession” fans — Kieran Culkin is shutting down any possibility of a spinoff once and for all.

	The actor, currently starring in “The Hu
body:
Sorry, “Succession” fans — Kieran Culkin is shutting down any possibility of a spinoff once and for all.

	The actor, currently starring in “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” as a young Caesar Flickerman, joined the “Heart Breakfast” radio show on Friday to discuss the new film, though hosts Amanda Holden and Jamie Theakston also snuck in a few questions regarding the hit HBO show’s potential future.


	“I know we’re not here to talk about this, but I’m still grieving the end of ‘Succession,’” said Holden, to which Culkin responded: “Oh, you are? Get over it. It’s been three years!” When asked about a potential for a spinoff, Culkin answered, “Of course not. I think that would be a terrible idea… I mean, what are you hoping for? ‘Cousin Greg: The Sitcom?’… Yeah, that would be a terrible idea.”
	

	And though the “A Real Pain” actor is steadfast about not retreading the show’s familiar territory, he noted that he misses playing Roman Roy and the “whole thing.”

	Culkin continued: “It was fun. It was one of those where Jesse Armstrong, the showrunner, spent the entire last season trying to figure out if there was a way to do one more. I never wanted to know what was going to happen in the season and on the fourth one I did ask and when he pitched me the end of the season and I went ‘well, that kind of sounds like it’s the end of the show.’ But when he pitched me three different ideas of what season 5 could be, they all sounded good… But it ended perfectly. The way it was supposed to.

	Elsewhere in the interview, Culkin divulged that he’ll be reuniting with “Succession” creator Jesse Armstrong on a new film. Culkin starred alongside Brian Cox, Sarah Snook, Jeremy Strong, Nicholas Braun, Matthew Macfadyen, Alan Ruck and more in the acclaimed drama, which ran for four seasons. 
	

	“The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” hit theaters on Friday and brought in $56 million on opening day.

schema.headline: Kieran Culkin Says a ‘Succession’ Spinoff ‘Would Be a Terrible Idea’: ‘What Are You Hoping For? “Cousin Greg: The Sitcom?”’

title: SXSW Forges Partnership With Egypt’s UTH Festival Dedicated to Youth Culture
description: Austin’s South by Southwest Film and TV Festival has forged a partnership with Egypt’s UTH Festival dedicated to youth culture under which UTH will
body:
Austin’s South by Southwest Film and TV Festival has forged a partnership with Egypt’s UTH Festival dedicated to youth culture under which UTH will become SXSW‘s partner in Egypt.

	The agreement is aimed at “identifying emerging talent and building opportunities for Egyptian filmmakers, musicians, creators, founders and business leaders to engage with SXSW’s international network,” according to a statement.


	The third edition of the just concluded UTH Festival just ran Nov. 20 and 21 at the Grand Egyptian Museum in Giza, on the west bank of the Nile opposite Cairo, attracting roughly 10,000 attendees, according to organizers. This year’s festival, held under the theme “Work in Progress,” covered fashion, design, creator economy, film, music, food and sports, among other spheres.
	

	The announcement stems from an initiative bringing SXSW and Egyptian industry figures together during the UTH fest, which was attended by Peter Lewis, who is SXSW’s chief commercial officer.

	As part of the collaboration, an Egyptian delegation comprising roughly 20 participants will travel to SXSW to attend the fest between March 13–21. Curated and led by UTH, the delegation will “bring together representatives from Egypt’s film and music industries, the creator economy, entrepreneurship, investment and institutional sectors,” according to the statement. The agreement also includes plans for “a UTH-led programming session and a community gathering in Austin,” the statement added.

	The collaboration also envisions possible Egyptian participation in the SXSW EDU program and SXSW London in 2027, with formats to be developed by the parties. Going forward, “UTH’s ambition is to establish an Egypt House at SXSW, providing a gathering place for Egyptian talent, companies and institutional partners in Austin,” according to the statement.
	

	“SXSW was founded to help creative people connect, launch new ideas, and shape the future,” Peter Lewis said in the statement. “We are excited to partner with the UTH Festival team, who share our vision to empower the next generation of compelling, visionary and diverse creative voices,” he added. “We look forward to working closely with UTH in Egypt, and welcoming leaders from Egypt’s business, entertainment and creative industries to Austin next March.”

	Commented Omar El Aawar, UTH Festival founder and CEO: “Egypt has no shortage of creative talent. What we need are more opportunities for that talent to connect with the global industry.” 

	El Aawar added: “Our partnership with SXSW is about building that bridge, creating real opportunities for Egyptian filmmakers, musicians, creators and entrepreneurs to take their work beyond our borders.” 

	“We want UTH to be more than a festival that brings people together for two days. We want to build a platform that opens doors throughout the year, and this partnership is an important step towards that ambition.”

	Pictured above: Omar El Aawar, founder and CEO of UTH (seated left); Peter Lewis, chief commercial officer of SXSW (seated right). DigiSay founder Ahmed Abbas (standing left) and UTH co-founder Ahmed Ragy (standing right).

schema.headline: SXSW Forges Partnership With Egypt’s UTH Festival Dedicated to Youth Culture

title: Jennifer Lopez Teases ‘Monster-in-Law’ Sequel With Jane Fonda: ‘We’re Talking About Maybe Doing Another One’
description:
Jennifer Lopez and Jane Fonda might reunite for a “Monster-in-Law” follow-up, the singer and actress teased recently. 

	In a clip from Lopez’s upc
body:
Jennifer Lopez and Jane Fonda might reunite for a “Monster-in-Law” follow-up, the singer and actress teased recently. 

	In a clip from Lopez’s upcoming appearance on “The Drew Barrymore Show,” she reminisced with the host about past projects, including the 2005 rom-com she starred in with Fonda.

	“I love this movie so much,” Barrymore said. “I love Jane. And Michael [Vartan],” Lopez said of her “Monster-in-Law” co-stars.
	

	The rom-com starred Fonda as Viola Fields, a mother-in-law-to-be determined to stop her son (Vartan) from marrying Charlotte “Charlie” Cantilini (Lopez). Monet Mazur, Wanda Sykes, Adam Scott, Annie Parisse and Will Arnett also starred.

	Lopez said working with Fonda was “amazing.” “I mean, loved her.” She added, “We’re talking about maybe doing another one.”

	Lopez and Fonda have remained close since filming “Monster-in-Law.” In 2013, Fonda spoke at Lopez’s Hollywood Walk of Fame ceremony, and the two reunited at a 2025 pre-Oscars party.

	Barrymore also showed the audience shots from Lopez’s Fonda-inspired Halloween costume from this year. “The Halloween Barbarella nod was as hot as it gets,” Barrymore said.

	“I don’t know what came over me,” Lopez said. “I was like, ‘Maybe I’ll get dressed up,’ and then I thought of Barbarella. It was a little tip to some of the music I’m making.” 

	Lopez’s appearance is in promotion of her new concert film, “The JLo Show,” created from Lopez’s final performance during her Las Vegas residency. The film premieres Nov. 26 on CBS and will stream on Paramount+. On Friday, the star made headlines for donning a 186-carat diamond necklace to the premiere.

schema.headline: Jennifer Lopez Teases ‘Monster-in-Law’ Sequel With Jane Fonda: ‘We’re Talking About Maybe Doing Another One’

title: Katseye Brings Out Camila Cabello for ‘Gabriela’ Dance at Los Angeles Show
description: Roughly six songs into their performance on Saturday night, Katseye made a girl group connection with Fifth Harmony member Camila Cabello as Daniel
body:
Roughly six songs into their performance on Saturday night, Katseye made a girl group connection with Fifth Harmony member Camila Cabello as Daniela Avanzini brought her out to be the collective’s “Gabriela” for the evening, dancing to the choreography that accompanies the song.

	Katseye, who performed as a quartet consisting of Avanzini alongside Lara Raj, Yoonchae and Megan Skindiel, took the stage at around 8:30 p.m. at Los Angeles’ Crypto.com Arena, running through opener “Hootie Frutti” and “Touch” before the girls exited so that Avanzini could bring out Cabello.
	

	“OK, you look stunning,” said Avanzini as Cabello joined her. “Thank you Camila, I have one question for you: Do you know the ‘Gabriela’ dance?”

	“I know a little bit, just a little bit,” responded Cabello. “We’re two Latina mamis, I feel like there’s a lot of Latina mamis in here. So even if we get steps wrong, it’s the sazon that counts.” They continued on to do the “Gabriela” dance, hitting the hand-ography before Cabello left the stage and the rest of Katseye joined back up to do a full performance of the single.

	Throughout the show, Katseye gave a tour of their discography from the past few years, including hits like “Pinky Up,” “Gnarly” and “Mean Girls.” Katseye, who was recently announced as the recipient of the Group of the Year Award at Variety Hitmakers’ 2026, is currently on its “Wildworld” tour amid a year that saw several members take temporary hiatuses to improve their mental health. Katseye will perform again at Crypto.com Arena on Sunday night before a show in Phoenix and a tour closer at Fort Worth, Texas’ Ariat Arena on December 1.

title: Neon-Backed Biopic ‘Caesar,’ About Syrian Officer Who Blew the Whistle on Assad Regime Torture, to Be Directed by Ameer Fakher Eldin
description: Ameer Fakher Eldin (“The Stranger,” “Yunan”) is set to direct Neon-backed biopic “Caesar.” The film centers on Syrian military officer Farid Al-Mad
body:
Ameer Fakher Eldin (“The Stranger,” “Yunan”) is set to direct Neon-backed biopic “Caesar.” The film centers on Syrian military officer Farid Al-Madhhan who blew the whistle on torture and killings perpetrated by the regime of Syrian president Bashar Assad. 

	Syrian star Taim Hassan has been cast in the lead role playing the film’s titular hero, who’s nom de guerre was Caesar. Farid Al-Madhhan was a military police photographer and head of the judicial evidence office in Damascus.
	

	Al-Madhhan launched a secret operation to smuggle more than 50,000 photographs out of Syria showing evidence of torture, starvation and murder in the country’s lockups. This evidence marked a turning point in Syrian history, prompting European prosecutors to take legal proceeding against the Assad government’s war crimes. 

	The dictator’s reign of terror ended in December 2024 after a 13-year civil war that caused more than 500,000 deaths and forced millions of Syrians to leave their homeland.

	Hassan has played the lead in hit Arabic TV show “Al Hayba,” about a family of arms smugglers working the border between Syria and Lebanon, a role that made him a household name across the region and reached international audiences on Netflix. His more recent work includes the show “Taj” (2024), in which he plays a boxer resisting the French occupation of Syria; hit political drama “Under the Seventh Ground” (2025); and thriller series “Mawlana” (2026).

	The high-end biopic was unveiled during an emotionally charged press conference held during the Industry Days of the Doha Film Festival, attended by a broad panel. The panel included both Taim Hassan, set to play Caesar, and the real Farid Al-Madhhan. (They are pictured above, from left to right).
	

	Al-Madhhan pointed out that the upcoming film about his act – which carried extreme danger of torture and murder by Syrian authorities – will not be “a forensic or documentary exercise.”

	“It is a human story – the story of people who had lives, families and experiences, but whose lives unfortunately ended in inhumane circumstances. That is why we decided to tell this story through cinema: to give a voice to the human beings who suffered,” he said.

	“Seeing the actor and the person he is portraying sitting together is quite remarkable,” noted U.S. producer Mike Larocca, co-founder of Department M. “It is like looking in a mirror,” he added. “I think we have managed to find the right actor.” 

	The “Caesar” project is being developed by Department M and Doha’s Katara Studios, with distribution in place via Neon and support from Kuwait-based studio Sard Media. Syrian production company Tadmor Film City is also on board. 

	BAFTA-nominated screenwriting duo Rory Haines and Sohrab Noshirvani (“The Mauritanian,” “Informer”) are on board to write the screenplay.

	Berlin-based helmer Ameer Fakher Eldin, who was born in Kyiv, Ukraine, to Syrian parents from the Golan Heights, said: “Caesar’s story carries enormous responsibility. Behind the scale of the events is the deeply human story of an individual confronted with an extraordinary choice, and the courage required to act when the consequences were almost unimaginable.”

	The project had been first announced during the first edition of the Doha Industry Days in 2025 by the Qatar Film Committee, an official body that is part of the Media City Qatar hub tasked with driving growth of the country’s entertainment industry.

	Commented Hassan Al Thawadi, the Qatari lawyer who chairs the Qatar Film Committee: “Caesar’s story is one of extraordinary courage, sacrifice and global consequence. When we announced this project last year, our ambition was to assemble a cast and creative team capable of approaching his story with the humanity, sensitivity and cinematic ambition it deserves.”

	Larocca at the press conference noted that “it is very rare for a film of this nature to receive the level of resources and support that we have received.” He thanked Al Thawadi and the other partners “for giving us the support necessary to attempt to make a film of the highest possible quality by international standards.”
	

	“I hope we will be back here next year to announce significant production milestones,” he said.

	The Doha Film Festival’s second edition runs Nov. 19-27 in the Qatari capital.

schema.headline: Neon-Backed Biopic ‘Caesar,’ About Syrian Officer Who Blew the Whistle on Assad Regime Torture, to Be Directed by Ameer Fakher Eldin

title: James Gray on Francis Ford Coppola’s Advice That Shaped His Career: ‘Be Personal. There’s Only One of You in This World’
description: When filmmaker James Gray was a teenager, he wrote a fan letter to Francis Ford Coppola. To his surprise, the legendary filmmaker wrote back with a
body:
When filmmaker James Gray was a teenager, he wrote a fan letter to Francis Ford Coppola. To his surprise, the legendary filmmaker wrote back with a piece of advice that would come to shape Gray’s entire approach to cinema.

	“He said, ‘Be personal, James. There’s only one of you in this world,’” Gray recalled during a press conference Sunday at the Doha Film Festival. “I’ve tried to take that to heart, that if I have anything to say at all, if I have a voice that matters at all, it’s best that I become as personal as I can.”
	

	Decades later, that philosophy remains central to Gray’s filmmaking, even as he argues that the film industry increasingly pressures directors to suppress their individual voices.

	“So much of the system, the systems in the cinema, both in the United States and abroad, try to discourage you from your own voice,” he said. “Or, if they don’t discourage you actively, they try to get you to bury your voice in a larger statement, or another form of genre, where it’s hidden.”

	The director was in Doha to present the MENA premiere of “Paper Tiger,” his latest crime drama starring Adam Driver, Miles Teller and Scarlett Johansson. Set in 1980s New York, the film follows two brothers whose pursuit of the American Dream draws them into a dangerous scheme involving the Russian mafia.

	Drawing heavily on his own family history, Gray described the film as an attempt to faithfully capture his father’s relationship with his uncle, while acknowledging the possible limitations of his own memory years later. He also recalled how a confrontation between his parents found its way into the film, with the actors recreating the incident almost exactly as it had unfolded in real life.
	

	Although “Paper Tiger” is framed as a crime drama, Gray said he does not think of his films primarily in terms of genre, which he sees as a way of categorizing cinema rather than defining its true purpose.

	“I’m just telling my story as best I can, as clearly as I can, as honestly as I can, and I hope for the best,” he said. For Gray, that commitment to honesty is also a means of fostering compassion and understanding. “That is how we extend the idea of compassion and sympathy in this world,” he explained. “Hopefully you can see something in me that matters to you.”

	“I have been very lucky to be able to pursue a cinema which is very directly personal,” he added. “So I don’t take it lightly. It’s a responsibility I take very seriously. And I think it’s actually the true calling of the filmmaker.”

	The conversation also turned to the future of independent cinema, with Brazilian producer Rodrigo Teixeira, whose “Paper Tiger” and “Furies” are both screening in Doha, pushing back against concerns about the dominance of Hollywood blockbusters.

	“You’re always going to have space to create original films outside of the system, because it’s impossible to own the whole system, even with all these mergers,” Teixeira said, citing companies such as A24 and Neon as examples of how independent filmmaking continues to thrive.

	Drawing a comparison between filmmaking in Brazil and the U.S., Teixeira argued that independent producers face much the same challenges regardless of geography. The principal difference, he said, is the public funding available in his home country, where federal support for cinema has long helped sustain the industry.

	“We have a government who supports cinema, who supports art,” he said, contrasting Brazil’s system with the U.S., where comparable government support is absent.

	Gray, meanwhile, recalled that he once believed cinema might follow the trajectory of opera, flourishing for roughly a century before eventually being eclipsed by another art form. While he acknowledged that cinema faces growing competition from video games and other forms of entertainment, and described the dominance of the blockbuster model as “overall quite harmful.” But the increasing accessibility of filmmaking technology has begun to challenge his earlier pessimism.
	

	“I have a kind of optimism about the availability of technology and how that will introduce new voices.”

schema.headline: James Gray on Francis Ford Coppola’s Advice That Shaped His Career: ‘Be Personal. There’s Only One of You in This World’

title: Karla Sofia Gascon Says ‘Emilia Perez’ Oscar Controversy Came From People Who ‘Didn’t Want Someone Like Me to Receive an Award’
description: Spanish actor Karla Sofia Gascon, whose turn in “Emilia Pérez” made her the first transgender actor to land an Oscar nomination, says the controver
body:
Spanish actor Karla Sofia Gascon, whose turn in “Emilia Pérez” made her the first transgender actor to land an Oscar nomination, says the controversy that consumed her awards campaign was driven by people who did not want to see someone like her win.

	“In reality, the controversy was generated by a great many people who didn’t want someone like me to receive an award,” Gascón tells Variety at the International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa, where her Spanish Western “Trinidad” is world premiering.
	

	Her Oscar run was overshadowed by a row over old social media posts. “It has never yet been shown that I wrote anything against anyone, nor has it been proven anywhere,” she says. “It was just a pile of assumptions, with everyone saying something different, and they created a figure of me that isn’t me.”

	Gascon describes a long awards push as an ordeal for actors, with political interests at play on every side, and says she would rather do her work and let audiences decide whether they like it. Such campaigns, she argues, open the door to people using actors for political or economic ends. “And I think we are here for the art,” she says.

	Cinema, in her view, carries a social responsibility to show audiences the best of humanity, even as it remains both entertainment and business. Mixing the political, the economic and the talent, she says, dilutes the essence of acting, which for her means bringing lives to other people and making them think.

	Transgender people face more and more problems, Gascón says. “We are living through a moment of regression in the rights of transgender people, of sexual diversity.”
	

	Global politics, Gascon adds, is making life harder still for people who already face steep odds, and above all for trans people, “who are considered in practically the whole world as the lowest in society.” That, she says, is why a campaign arose against “a woman who could win a great award” – a reading she stresses is “not a justification” but “an explanation.”

	“Emilia Perez,” directed by Jacques Audiard, won Gascon best actress at the Cannes Film Festival, the European Film Awards and the Lumiere Awards, alongside Golden Globe and BAFTA nominations. The biggest change to her career since, she says, is that she no longer has to audition. “I started at 16, I’ve had a career of more than 30 years and I’ve done everything in acting,” she says.

	She has since made the Italian film “Scuola di Seduzione” and “Trinidad.” On working across languages and cultures, she says: “It makes me grow as a person, it makes me grow in my work, it makes me understand human beings much more.”

	Next up is “Las Malas,” Armando Bo’s adaptation of Camila Sosa Villada’s novel, in which she plays Tia Encarna and which she rates among the best work of her life. The film shot for around four months this year in Argentina and Uruguay. Gascon sees many parallels with “Emilia Perez” in the role but would rather discuss it once audiences have seen it, possibly at Cannes or Venice.

	During a masterclass at the festival, where she was honored by Chanchal Kumar, secretary of India’s Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, Gascon detailed her “Trinidad” character: a gun-wielding outlaw who uses a wheelchair and serves as the villain of the 19th-century tale. She had hoped for horses and guns when the Western came calling, only to learn she would be playing a woman “in a chair without any movement.”

	“And when you confront this, you say, ‘That’s the best opportunity for me to understand other people in this world,'” she told the audience.

	Gascon builds every role from the voice outward, seeking a “really soft, really calm” register for the “Trinidad” role. On “Emilia Pérez,” she recorded a range of voices on cassette before settling on a deep voice for Manitas and a “delicate” one for Emilia, and came to appreciate the process when dubbing herself later.

	She called Audiard the best director she has worked with. “He brings you the liberty to act,” Gascón said. “He plays a lot, he laughs a lot, he’s really funny, and I think he is a really good friend.”
	

	On set, she said, actors should remember they are one part of a team that can run to hundreds. “I don’t want to create conflict on set. I don’t want to create a difference between me and the others. I don’t want blue flowers in my caravan,” she said.

	Gascon traced her affection for India to a Madrid screening of Deepa Mehta’s “Water” decades ago, and named Indian Oscar winner A.R. Rahman her favorite musician. She also drew parallels between the heightened performance styles of Mexican telenovelas, where she spent much of her career, and Indian cinema, arguing that histrionics and truth are compatible.

	She also said filmmakers too often cast to labels such as “Spanish” or “she is a woman” instead of trusting actors’ range. “It’s nice when Indian people work in Spain, work in the United States. I love when a Russian works in Africa,” Gascon said. “I think we are all the same humanity.”

              '90 Day Fiancé' star Sheila Mangubat has died just days before her 36th birthday.
      
    
              Sheila's former fiancé David Dangerfield shared the news on Instagram, writing ... "It breaks my heart to share the news from her family that Sheila passed away on Saturday in the Philippines. I am devastated and still trying to process this loss."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
              Sheila's brother Jonathan also shared a video of her funeral Sunday to his Facebook stories ... hours after posting a clip of him and his family mourning her on her deathbed.
      

              Despite breaking up in Oct. 2025 after years of going long-distance and K-1 visa setbacks ... David said he had rekindled his romance with Sheila in June 2026.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
              As you know ... David and Sheila connected on a Facebook group for deaf singles.
      
    
              Their romance and engagement were featured on Season 6 of "90 Day Fiancé: Before the 90 Days."
      
    
              Sheila was 35 years old.

title: Titans' Jaylen Harrell Car Crash: Hospitalized & Under Investigation For Allegedly Assaulting Driver, Report
description:

                          Investigated After Alleged Assault
body:
Titans’ Jaylen Harrell Hospitalized
                          Investigated After Alleged Assault of Rideshare Driver
                          ... Before Crash
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 22, 2026
                            7:12 AM PST
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              Jaylen Harrell -- a defensive end on the Tennessee Titans -- has been hospitalized following a car crash ... and police claim he allegedly assaulted a rideshare driver before the collision.
      
    
              The Tampa PD are investigating the crash after alleging that while Jaylen was a passenger in the car, "he reportedly assaulted the driver while the vehicle was in motion" in Tampa Friday morning ... ESPN reported.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              Police claim the driver swerved as a result, struck another car before hitting a pole ... sending Harrell into the windshield, causing him to lose consciousness.
      

              Harrell has since been transported to a local hospital with serious injuries ... and the Titans have said that he "remains in the hospital and continues to receive care," per Fox News.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              It's unclear what his current medical status is ... while the rideshare driver only suffered minor injuries, according to cops.
      
    
              We've reached out to the Tampa Police and Harrell's rep for comment ... so far, no word back.
